narrative:
The model predicted a 61% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven by three key factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of accepted students, signaling that your later academic performance was not as competitive as most successful applicants.

Next in importance was your LSAT score. At 33, it fell below the average of 37 among accepted students and also pulled the prediction toward a higher risk of failing the bar.

Working in the opposite direction, your undergraduate GPA of 3.9 was the third most influential factor and worked in your favor. It is substantially higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and helped reduce the predicted risk of failure.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of your later class standing and LSAT score outweighed the positive signal from your strong college grades, resulting in a failure probability high enough to deny admission.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score, while also strengthening your performance in any remaining coursework. Improving either of those two areas would likely shift future predictions in your favor and improve your chances of admission. (218 words)
